questions.prompt: In C++20, is the declaration of `n` well-formed?
options: Yes: `NoDefault` is an aggregate, so `{}` never calls the constructor
Yes: `n.x` is zero-initialized
No: the type is not an aggregate, so `{}` calls the deleted default constructor
Yes in C++20, but it was ill-formed in C++17
questions.explanation: Since C++20 (P1008) a class with any user-declared constructor is not an aggregate, and a deleted constructor is user-declared. Empty braces on a class with a default constructor value-initialize, which selects the deleted constructor, so the program is ill-formed. The first option was true in C++11 through C++17, where only user-provided constructors disqualified a type, so the code compiled; the last option has the history backwards.

questions.prompt: In C++20, is this declaration well-formed?
questions.code:
struct P { int x, y; };

P p{.y = 1, .x = 2};
options: No: designators must appear in declaration order
Yes: `p.x` is 2 and `p.y` is 1, as in C
Yes: the values are applied positionally, so `p.x` is 1
Yes, but the order in which `x` and `y` are initialized is unspecified
questions.explanation: C++20 designated initializers must name members in the order they are declared, so this is ill-formed. C accepts any order, which makes the second option tempting, and Clang accepts it as an extension with a `-Wreorder-init-list` warning; GCC rejects it. The rule exists so that initializers are evaluated in the same order as members are initialized.

It does not compile: `c` needs an initializer
questions.explanation: `Opts` is an aggregate (default member initializers are allowed since C++14). Elements without an initializer use their default member initializer, so `b` is 5, and otherwise are copy-initialized from an empty initializer list, which zeroes `c`. The indeterminate answer would be right for `Opts o;`, which default-initializes, but any brace list makes every element initialized.

options: Yes: it creates `P{1, 2}` and `P{3, 4}`
No: `{1, 2}` initializes the inner array, so `{3, 4}` is an excess initializer
Yes, but `a[1]` is value-initialized and `{3, 4}` is ignored
No: `std::array` cannot be initialized from nested braces
questions.explanation: `std::array<P, 2>` is a struct whose single element is a built-in `P[2]`. The first clause `{1, 2}` is a braced list, so it initializes that inner array, as `P[2]{1, 2}`, filling `a[0]`. The second clause has no element left to initialize, so the program is ill-formed. Brace elision only helps when you elide all the inner braces, `{1, 2, 3, 4}`, or write all of them, `{{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}}`.

questions.prompt: In C++20, what does the standard say about this program?
options: It returns 84
It is ill-formed: an aggregate with a reference member cannot be initialized with parentheses
The behavior is undefined: `b.r` refers to a temporary that has been destroyed
The behavior is undefined: both `a.r` and `b.r` dangle
questions.explanation: Both declarations are aggregate initialization; the parenthesized form is valid since C++20. With braces, the temporary bound to the reference member is lifetime-extended to the lifetime of `a`. [class.temporary] makes an exception for an aggregate initialized from a parenthesized expression-list, so the temporary behind `b.r` dies at the end of that declaration and reading it is undefined behavior. That asymmetry is why the first option is so tempting.

questions.prompt: In C++20, is the declaration of `b` well-formed?
options: No: `Open` is an aggregate, and `Guarded()` is not accessible where the base is initialized
Yes: `Open`'s implicit default constructor calls `Guarded()`
Yes: a derived class may always call a protected base constructor
It is implementation-defined
questions.explanation: Since C++17 a class with a public base can be an aggregate, so `Open{}` is aggregate initialization and the base element is copy-initialized from `{}` in the context of `main`, where the protected constructor is inaccessible. The program is ill-formed. Before C++17 `Open` was not an aggregate and its implicit constructor called `Guarded()` from inside the derived class, which is what the second option describes; `Open b;` still works that way.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an aggregate in C++20?
options: `struct A { private: int x; };`
`struct B { B() = default; int x; };`
The closure type of `[] {}`
`struct D : Base { int d; void f(); ~D(); };` where `Base` is a class with only public members
questions.explanation: Member functions and a user-declared destructor never disqualify a class, and since C++17 a public non-virtual base is allowed, so `D` is an aggregate. A private non-static data member disqualifies `A`. `B` has a user-declared constructor, which disqualifies it since C++20 even though it is defaulted, the tempting answer for anyone who learned the C++17 rule. The standard states outright that a closure type is not an aggregate.

questions.prompt: In C++20, with no deduction guides declared, what is `decltype(p)`?
options: The declaration is ill-formed: there is no constructor or guide to deduce from
`Pair<int, double>`
`Pair<double, double>`
`Pair<int, int>`
questions.explanation: C++20 adds an aggregate deduction candidate: for an aggregate class template, the compiler synthesizes a candidate whose parameters are the element types, so `T` deduces from `1` and `U` from `2.0`. In C++17 deduction failed here unless you wrote a guide, which is the first option and the reason `std::array` ships with one.
